title: Private deploy egress: DNS/TLS breadcrumbs and quick experiments
content:
Summary:
- Intermittent outbound failures from private deployment to model-hosting endpoints (api.models.example.com), surfaced as TLS handshake errors & timeouts. Impact: ~10-20% request error rate during peak 08:00–10:00 PST on 2025-02-14.
- Suspected corollary: DNS resolution sometimes returning unexpected internal IPs (10.0.0.0/8) or timing out and then client falls back to cached IP that routes through peering path that drops TCP 443.

Observed behavior and timeline (quick bullet timeline):
- 07:58: first anomaly alert: 5xx from gateway for external callouts.
- 08:05: manual curl on affected node: hangs ~8s then returns TLS handshake failure.
- 08:10: noticed high DNS latency on node (dig @10.0.1.2 api.models.example.com  +short ~ 2s occasionally).
- 08:22: after restarting dnsmasq on edge-router, error rate dropped for ~30m then crept back up.
- 09:05: tcpdump on egress showed a flurry of DNS A queries followed by TCP SYNs with RSTs from peer side for some flows.

Commands run (snippets + notable outputs):
- dig (from app pod):
  dig @10.0.1.2 api.models.example.com +time=2 +tries=1
  ;; Query time: 1992 msec
  ;; ANSWER SECTION:
  api.models.example.com.  60 IN A 34.210.55.82

- repeated dig to internal DNS server: occasional no answer or SERVFAIL
  dig @10.0.1.2 api.models.example.com
  ;; -> ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

- tcpdump capture (abridged):
  08:12:04.123456 IP 10.0.3.14.49012 > 34.210.55.82.443: Flags [S], seq 0, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 12345 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
  08:12:04.203112 IP 34.210.55.82.443 > 10.0.3.14.49012: Flags [RST, ACK], seq 0, ack 1, win 0, length 0
  (multiple similar flows)

- openssl s_client:
  openssl s_client -connect api.models.example.com:443 -servername api.models.example.com -timeout 5
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  140377...:error:14077410:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:sslv3 alert handshake failure
  ---
  no peer certificate available

- traceroute (from edge-router):
  traceroute to 34.210.55.82 (34.210.55.82), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
   1  10.0.1.1 (10.0.1.1)  0.272 ms  0.234 ms  0.209 ms
   2  198.51.100.1 (198.51.100.1)  5.123 ms  6.456 ms  5.987 ms
   3  34.210.55.82 (34.210.55.82)  8.123 ms  8.101 ms  8.089 ms

- ip route / ip rule (on node):
  ip route show table main: default via 10.0.1.254 dev eth0 proto static metric 100

- conntrack peek (on router):
  conntrack -L | grep 34.210.55.82
  tcp      6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.0.3.14 dst=34.210.55.82 sport=49012 dport=443 packets=12 bytes=984
  tcp      6 29 SYN_SENT src=10.0.3.15 dst=34.210.55.82 sport=51018 dport=443

Notes about these outputs:
- RST from remote IP (34.210.55.82) immediately after SYN suggests remote actively refusing the connection or path mangling (SYN arrives but remote thinks it is not valid e.g. due to missing TLS SNI or unexpected source IP).
- The TLS alert on openssl is "handshake failure" (alert 40) which can happen if ALPN/SNI mismatch or middlebox terminates or client offers unsupported versions/ciphers.
- Occasional DNS SERVFAIL or TCP timeout on DNS server increases likelihood of fallback to stale cache -> clients reuse older IPs that may now be served by a different regional host that rejects our source ASN/ips.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Intermittent upstream NAT/load-balancer blackholing for certain source ports or source IPs when requests cross peered path (peering asymmetry or ACLs at partner). Explains RST and immediate connection failures.
2) DNS queries sometimes resolve through internal resolver that returns private/legacy A records for example.com (split-horizon misconfig), causing traffic to go to an internal gateway which rejects TLS.
3) Path MTU or TCP MSS clamping causing TLS handshake fragmentation leading to handshake failure alerts.
4) A middlebox on egress (proxy/inspection) is dropping or resetting TLS handshakes intermittently when DNS took >1s (timing correlation).
5) Ephemeral port exhaustion / conntrack limit on router causing SYNs to be dropped / RSTs generated.

Experiments & quick mitigations attempted and outcome:
- Restarted dnsmasq on peering-router (08:22) -> temporary improvement (~30 min). Suggests DNS component involvement.
- Forced DNS to public resolver (8.8.8.8) for test pod by overriding /etc/resolv.conf -> success: TLS handshakes succeed consistently for 15m.
- Temporarily SNAT all outbound 443 from problematic nodes via specific egress IP (iptables MASQUERADE -> SNAT) -> error rate dropped to <1% while active.
- Increased conntrack table size by +20% (sysctl tweak) -> no immediate effect, but marginally fewer SYN_SENT states.

Interpretation of experiment outcomes:
- DNS change working -> strong signal that internal resolver or split-horizon is part of problem. Public DNS made remote IP resolution stable and removed misrouted flows.
- SNAT working -> if source IP mattered to remote (partner blocking unknown subnets) then SNAT fixes; supports hypothesis #1.

Reproduction steps for on-call to run quickly:
1) From affected pod: dig @10.0.1.2 api.models.example.com +tries=1 +time=2. Note latency and SERVFAIL.
2) If SERVFAIL, try dig @8.8.8.8 api.models.example.com and compare IPs.
3) Run: openssl s_client -connect $(dig +short api.models.example.com):443 -servername api.models.example.com -timeout 5 and capture stderr.
4) On router: tcpdump -i eth0 host 34.210.55.82 and watch for RSTs after SYNs.
5) Check conntrack counts: cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count and nf_conntrack_max.

Next actions (short list):
- Short term (by EOD): keep SNAT workaround on for the problematic hostpool and route DNS to stable public resolvers for selected nodes. Communicate to infra team.
- Mid term: audit internal DNS servers for split-horizon entries for api.models.example.com and any stale A records; correlate with CDNs/backends ownership.
- Mid term: add synthetic probe from private deployment that runs dig to internal resolver and public resolver every 30s and reports divergence.
- Long term: create peering test harness with per-port NAT behavior tests, and run during peak window to reproduce.
- Ops: open ticket with peering partner (include SYN/RST tcpdumps and timestamps) to confirm whether they drop based on source IP/port ranges.

Notes-to-self / things we forgot to try:
- Capture full pcap across the moment dnsmasq restart happened (we only captured after).
- Verify if any firewall ACLs on partner side were recently updated around 2025-02-14 06:00 UTC.
- Check for kernel TLS offload changes on router (recent package updates were applied on 2025-02-12).

Useful snippets to paste in ticket: (copy/paste friendly)
- Example tcpdump line: 08:12:04.203112 IP 34.210.55.82.443 > 10.0.3.14.49012: Flags [RST, ACK]
- openssl error: error:14077410:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:sslv3 alert handshake failure
- dig timeout example: ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

Confidence: ~70% that DNS + source-IP NATing are the root contributors.

Questions for Diego / Lin:
- Diego: can you check if any peering ACLs changed on 2025-02-13/14?
- Lin: can you run probe with public DNS+no SNAT for a full hour during peak and capture pcap?

Checklist for follow-up email to infra and partner ops:
- Attach pcap and tcpdump snippets, conntrack snapshots, timestamps in UTC, example failing request ids.
- Describe temporary SNAT mitigation and request partner to search their logs for matching SYNs/RSTs.

Random notes and heuristics:
- When DNS latency spikes, client libs often fall back to cached IPs in ways that bypass normal egress routing and create weird source IPs.
- Middleboxes occasionally respond with RSTs rather than dropping which is helpful for fingerprinting.

End of scratchpad.

(Will trim and formalize into a ticket once Diego confirms peering ACLs).
